en.content: The oxidation state of sulphur in $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{S}_2 \mathrm{O}_7$ is
en.explanation:
To determine the oxidation state of sulfur in $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{S}_2 \mathrm{O}_7$, consider the following steps:

Write the Oxidation States of Known Atoms:

Hydrogen (H) generally has an oxidation state of +1.

Oxygen (O) generally has an oxidation state of -2.

Set Up the Equation:

In the compound $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{S}_2 \mathrm{O}_7$, the total oxidation states must sum to zero because it is a neutral molecule.

Let $x$ be the oxidation state of sulfur (S).

The oxidation state equation based on the compound is:

$$2(+1) + 2(x) + 7(-2) = 0.$$

Solve for $x$:

Calculate the contributions from hydrogen and oxygen:

Hydrogen: $2(+1) = +2$

Oxygen: $7(-2) = -14$

Plug these values into the equation:

$$+2 + 2x - 14 = 0.$$

Simplify the equation:

$$2x - 12 = 0.$$

Solve for $x$:

$$2x = 12$$

$$x = 6.$$

Thus, the oxidation state of sulfur in $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{S}_2 \mathrm{O}_7$ is +6. This corresponds to Option B: +6.

en.content: What is the density of water vapour at boiling point of water?
en.explanation:
At the boiling point of water, which is $100^\circ \mathrm{C}$ or $373 \, \mathrm{K}$, the density of water vapor can be calculated using the ideal gas law. The ideal gas law is given by:

$$ PV = nRT $$

Where:

$ P $ is the pressure (at boiling point, $ P $ is approximately $1 \, \mathrm{atm}$ or $101325 \, \mathrm{Pa}$)

$ V $ is the volume

$ n $ is the number of moles

$ R $ is the ideal gas constant ($8.314 \, \mathrm{J} \cdot \mathrm{mol}^{-1} \cdot \mathrm{K}^{-1}$)

$ T $ is the temperature in Kelvin

The density $\rho$ of a gas is related to its mass and volume:

$$ \rho = \frac{m}{V} $$

Where $ m $ is the mass. Additionally, the mass of the vapor can be represented as the molar mass $ M $ times the number of moles $ n $:

$$ m = nM $$

Substituting $ m = nM $ into the density equation and combining it with the ideal gas law, we get:

$$ \rho = \frac{nM}{V} = \frac{PM}{RT} $$

For water vapor, the molar mass $ M $ is approximately $18.015 \, \mathrm{g/mol}$. Plugging in the values:

$ P = 101325 \, \mathrm{Pa} $

$ M = 18.015 \, \mathrm{g/mol} $

$ R = 8.314 \, \mathrm{J} \cdot \mathrm{mol}^{-1} \cdot \mathrm{K}^{-1} $

$ T = 373 \, \mathrm{K} $

The calculation becomes:

$$ \rho = \frac{101325 \times 18.015}{8.314 \times 373} \, \mathrm{g} \cdot \mathrm{m}^{-3} $$

Simplifying, this gives:

$$ \rho \approx 0.598 \, \mathrm{g/m}^3 \approx 6 \times 10^{-4} \, \mathrm{g/cm}^3 $$

Thus, the density of water vapor at the boiling point of water is best approximated by:

Option C: $6 \times 10^{-4} \, \mathrm{g} \cdot \mathrm{cm}^{-3}$

en.content: In a bionomial distribution, mean is 18 and variance is 12 then $p=$ ...........
en.explanation:
In a binomial distribution, the mean ($\mu$) and variance ($\sigma^2$) are given by the formulas:

$$ \mu = np $$

$$ \sigma^2 = np(1-p) $$

where $ n $ is the number of trials and $ p $ is the probability of success in each trial.

Given:

Mean, $\mu = 18$

Variance, $\sigma^2 = 12$

Substituting the mean into the formula, we have:

$$ 18 = np $$

For the variance, substitute and rearrange:

$$ 12 = np(1-p) $$

Now, we solve these two equations simultaneously.

From the mean:

$$ n = \frac{18}{p} $$

Substitute $ n $ from Equation 1 into Equation 2:

$$ 12 = \left(\frac{18}{p}\right)p(1-p) $$

Simplify the expression:

$$ 12 = 18(1-p) $$

$$ 12 = 18 - 18p $$

Rearrange and solve for $ p $:

$$ 18p = 18 - 12 $$

$$ 18p = 6 $$

$$ p = \frac{6}{18} $$

$$ p = \frac{1}{3} $$

Thus, $ p = \frac{1}{3} $.

The correct option is Option B: $\frac{1}{3}$.

en.content: If lines $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{3}=\frac{z-1}{4}$ and $\frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-\lambda}{2}=\frac{z}{1}$ intersect each other, then $\lambda=\ldots \ldots$

and $\frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-\lambda}{2}=\frac{z}{1}=\lambda_2$ (let) ... (ii)

Then, any point on line (i) is $\left(2 \lambda_1+1,3 \lambda_1-1,4 \lambda_1+1\right)$ and any point on line (ii) is $\left(\lambda_2+3,2 \lambda_2+\lambda, \lambda_2\right)$

Clearly, then lines (i) and (ii) will intersect if $$\left(2 \lambda_1+1,3 \lambda_1-1,4 \lambda_1+1\right)=\left(\lambda_2+3,2 \lambda_2+\lambda, \lambda_2\right)$$

For some particular value of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$

$$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad 2 \lambda_1+1=\lambda_2+3,3 \lambda_1-1=2 \lambda_2+\lambda \\ & \text { and } 4 \lambda_1+1=\lambda_2 \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \lambda_1-\lambda_2=2,3 \lambda_1-2 \lambda_2=\lambda+1 \text { and } 4 \lambda_1-\lambda_2=-1 \end{aligned}$$

On solving $2 \lambda_1-\lambda_2=2$ and $4 \lambda_1-\lambda_2=-1$ We get $\lambda_1=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $\lambda_2=-5$

Now, putting the values of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ in

$$\begin{array}{rlrl} & 3 \lambda_1-2 \lambda_2 =\lambda+1 \\ \Rightarrow & 3\left(\frac{-3}{2}\right)-2(-5) =\lambda+1 \Rightarrow \frac{-9}{2}+10=\lambda+1 \\ \Rightarrow & \lambda+1 =\frac{11}{2} \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{9}{2} \end{array}$$

en.content: Two pendulums begin to swing simultaneously. The first pendulum makes nine full oscillations when the other makes seven. The ratio of the lengths of the two pendulums is
en.explanation:
As two pendulums begin to swing simultaneously, then

$$n_1 T_1=n_2 T_2\quad\text{.... (i)}$$

where, $n_1$ and $n_2$ are the number of oscillations of first and second pendulum respectively and $T_1$ and $T_2$ be their respective time periods.

The time period of simple pendulum is given by

$T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$

where, $I=$ length of pendulum

and $g=$ acceleration due to gravity

$\Rightarrow \quad T^2 \propto l\quad\text{.... (ii)}$

So, from Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get

$$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{l_1}{l_2}=\frac{(7)^2}{(9)^2}=\frac{49}{81}$$

Hence, the ratio of pendulum lengths $I_1: I_2=49: 81$.

en.content: When light enters glass from vacuum, then the wavelength of light

en.content: What is the minimum energy required to launch a satellite of mass ' $m$ ' from the surface of the earth of mass ' $M$ ' and radius ' $R$ ' at an altitude $2 R$ ?

en.content: In a parallel plate air capacitor the distance between plates is reduced to one fourth and the space between them is filled with a dielectric medium of constant 2 . If the initial capacity of the capacitor is $4 \mu \mathrm{~F}$. then its new capacity is
en.explanation:
The capacitance of a parallel plate air capacitor is given by

$$C_0=\frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\quad\text{.... (i)}$$

where, $\varepsilon_0=$ permittivity of the medium,

$A=$ area of plates

and $\quad d=$ distance between the plates

When the distance between plates is reduced and a dielectric slab is introduced, then the capacitance becomes

$C=\frac{K \varepsilon_0 A}{d_1}\quad\text{.... (ii)}$

Where, $K=$ dielectric constant of medium.

Here, $K=2, d_1=\frac{d}{4}$ and $C_0=4 \mu \mathrm{~F}=4 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~F}$

From Eq. (ii), we get

$$\begin{aligned} C & =4\left(\frac{K \varepsilon_0 A}{d_1}\right)=4 K\left(\frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\right) \\ & =4 K C_0\quad\text{.... (iii) [from Eq. (i)]} \end{aligned}$$

Substituting given values in Eq. (iii), we get

$$C=4 \times 2 \times 4=32 \mu \mathrm{~F}$$

en.content: An aircraft is moving with uniform velocity $150 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ in the space. If all the forces acting on it are balanced, then it will
en.explanation: As all the forces acting on the aircraft are balanced, so the net force on it will be zero, i.e., no external force act on it. Thus, the aircraft will keep moving with the same velocity of $150 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ in the space.

en.content: In case of $p$-n junction diode, the width of depletion region is
en.explanation: In case of $p-n$ junction diode, when it is reverse biased, the reverse voltage supports the barrier potential and hence the width of the depletion layer increases. In forward biasing, the width decreases as the forward voltage opposes the potential barrier. The width of the depletion region increases, if the diode is further doped heavily as the movement of charge carrier decreases. Also, when the $p-n$ junction is light doped, the width of depletion region increases, due to increase in the potential barrier.

en.content: In the study of transistor as an amplifier, the ratio of collector current to emitter current is 0.98 then the ratio of collector current to base current will be
en.explanation:
The ratio of collector current to emitter current at constant collector base voltage is the current the amplification factor and given by

$$\alpha=\frac{I_C}{I_E}=0.98\quad\text{(given)}$$

The ratio of collector current to the base current at constant collector-emitter voltage is given by

$$\beta=\frac{I_C}{I_B}$$

These are related as $\beta=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}$

$$\Rightarrow \quad \beta=\frac{0.98}{1-0.98}=\frac{0.98}{0.02}=49$$

en.content: A stretched wire of length 260 cm is set into vibrations. It is divided into three segments whose frequencies are in the ratio $2: 3: 4$. Their lengths must be
en.explanation:
The frequency produced by a stretched wire is given by

$$f=\frac{p}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{m}}\quad\text{.... (i)}$$

where, $p=$ number of loops formed in vibration,

$l=$ length of wire,

$T=$ tension in wire,

and $m=$ mass per unit length of wire

So, from Eq (i), we get

$$f \propto \frac{1}{l}$$

Here, the ratio of frequencies of three segment is

$$\begin{aligned} & f_1: f_2: f_3=2: 3: 4 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad l_1: l_2: l_3=\frac{1}{2}: \frac{1}{3}: \frac{1}{4} \\ & =6: 4: 3 \end{aligned}$$

The length of wire, $L=260 \mathrm{~cm}$, so

$$\begin{aligned} l_1 & =\frac{6}{13} \times 260=120 \mathrm{~cm} \\ l_2 & =\frac{4}{13} \times 260=80 \mathrm{~cm} \\ \text { and } \quad l_3 & =\frac{3}{13} \times 260=60 \mathrm{~cm} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: The force ' $F$ ' acting on a body of density ' $d$ ' are related by the relation $F=\frac{y}{\sqrt{d}}$. The dimensions of ' $y$ ' are

en.content: The magnetization of bar magnet of length 5 cm , cross sectional area $2 \mathrm{~cm}^2$ and net magnetic moment $1 \mathrm{Am}^2$ is

en.content: Which of the following molecules is a polar molecule?

en.content: A simple harmonic progressive wave is represented as $y=0.03 \sin \pi(2 t-0.01 x) \mathrm{m}$. At a given instant of time, the phase difference between two particles 25 m apart is
en.explanation:

en.content: The equation of state for 2 g of oxygen at a pressure ' $P$ ' and temperature ' $T$, when occupying a volume ' $V$ ' will be

en.content: The magnetic dipole moment of a short magnetic dipole at a distant point along the equator of magnet has a magnitude of ' $X$ ' in SI units. If the distance between the point and the magnet is halved then the magnitude of dipole moment will be

en.content: The ratio of the dimensions of Planck's constant to that of moment of inertia is the dimensions of
en.explanation:
The dimensions of Planck's constant,

$$[\mathrm{h}]=\frac{[\mathrm{E}]}{[\mathrm{v}]}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{M}^0 \mathrm{~L}^0 \mathrm{~T}^{-1}\right]}=\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-1}\right]$$

and that moment of inertia,

$$\begin{aligned} & {[I]=[M][R]^2=[M][L]^2=\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^0\right]} \\ \therefore\quad & \frac{[\mathrm{h}]}{[I]}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-1}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^0\right]}=\left[\mathrm{T}^{-1}\right]=[\nu] \end{aligned}$$

Thus, the ratio of dimensions of Planck's constant to that at moment of inertia is the dimensions of frequency.

en.content: If ' $x$ ', $v$ ' and ' $a$ ' denote the displacement, velocity and acceleration of a particle respectively executing SHM of periodic time $h$ then which one of the following does not change with time?
en.explanation:
The dimensions of given variables of SHM are as

Displacement, $[x]=\left[M^0 L T^0\right]$

Velocity, $$[\mathrm{v}]=\left[\mathrm{M}^0 \mathrm{LT}^{-1}\right]$$

Acceleration, $[a]=\left[M^0 L T^{-2}\right]$

and time period, $[T]=\left[M^0 L^0 T\right]$

Now, checking each option for these values

For option (a)

$$\frac{[a][T]}{[x]}=\frac{\left[M^0 L T^{-2}\right]\left[M^0 L^0 T\right]}{\left[M^0 L T^0\right]}=\left[M^0 L^0 T^{-1}\right]$$

As it depends on time, so change with it.

For option (b),

$$\begin{aligned} {[a][T]+2 \pi[v] } & =\left[M^0 L T^{-2}\right]\left[M^0 L^0 T\right]+\left[M^0 L^0 T^{-1}\right] \\ & =\left[M^0 L T^{-1}\right] \end{aligned}$$

It is also dependent on time and hence changes with it.

For option (c),

$$\frac{[a][T]}{[v]}=\frac{\left[M^0 L T^{-2}\right]\left[M^0 L^0 T\right]}{\left[M^0 L T^{-1}\right]}=\left[M^0 L^0 T^0\right]$$

As it is a constant having no dimension, so it does not change with time.

For option (d),

$$\begin{aligned} \text { [a] }[t]+4 \pi^2[d]^2 & =\left[M^\rho L T^{-2}\right]\left[M^0 L^0 T\right]+\left[M^0 L T^{-1}\right]^2 \\ & =\left[L T^{-1}\right]+\left[L^2 T^{-2}\right] \end{aligned}$$

As, the term is dependent on time, so changes with it.

Also, it is dimensionally incorrect.

Hence, option (c) is correct.

en.content: A particle is performing U.C.M. along the circumference of a circle of diameter 50 cm with frequency 2 Hz . The acceleration of the particle in $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ is
en.explanation:

en.content: Find the wrong statement from the following about the equation of stationary wave given by $Y=0.04 \cos (\pi x) \sin (50 \pi t) \mathrm{m}$ where $t$ is in second. Then for the stationary wave.
en.explanation:
The given equation of wave is

Thus, the given wave is the combination of two waves,

$$\begin{array}{ll} y_1=0.02 \sin (50 \pi t+\pi x) & \text { (in -ve } x \text {-direction) } \\ \text { and } y_2=0.02 \sin (50 \pi t-\pi x) & \text { (in +ve } x \text {-direction) } \end{array}$$

Comparing them with the general equation of wave a $\sin (\omega t+k x)$, we get

Amplitude, $\quad a=0.02 \mathrm{~m}$

Time period, $T=\frac{2 \pi}{50 \pi}=\frac{1}{25}=0.04 \mathrm{~s}$

Wavelength, $\lambda=\frac{2 \pi}{\pi}=2 \mathrm{~m}$

So, option (a) is wrong.

en.content: A convex lens of focal length ' $f$ ' is placed in contact with a concave lens of the same focal length. The equivalent focal length of the combination is

Substituting given value in Eq. (i), we get

Hence, the equivalent focal length of the combination is infinity.

en.content: The range of an ammeter of resistance ' $G$ can be increased from ' $I$ ' to ' $nI$ ' by connecting
en.explanation:

en.content: The critical angle for light going from medium ' $x^{\prime}$ to medium ' $y$ ' is ' $\theta$ '. The speed of light in medium ' $x$ ' is ' $v_x$ '. The speed of light in medium ' $y$ ' is
en.explanation:
The critical angle is that angle on incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in rarer medium is $90^{\circ}$, i.e.

$$\begin{aligned} \quad & \frac{\sin \theta}{\sin 90^{\circ}}=\frac{\mu_y}{\mu_x} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \sin \theta=\frac{\mu_y}{\mu_x}\quad\text{.... (i)} \end{aligned}$$

where, $\mu=$ refractive index of medium.

Also, $\mu=\frac{\text { speed of light in vacuum }}{\text { speed of light in medium }}=\frac{c}{v}\quad\text{.... (ii)}$

From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get

$$\sin \theta=\frac{c}{v_y} \times \frac{v_x}{c}=\frac{v_x}{v_y} \Rightarrow v_y=\frac{v_x}{\sin \theta}$$

Thus, the speed of light in medium $y$ is $\frac{v_x}{\sin \theta}$.

en.content: When a 12000 joule of work is done on a flywheel, its frequency of rotation increases from 10 Hz to 20 Hz . The moment of inertia of flywheel about its axis of rotation is $\left(\pi^2=10\right)$
en.explanation:
Given, work done, $W=12000 \mathrm{~J}$,

Initial frequency, $f_1=10 \mathrm{~Hz}$

and final frequency, $f_2=20 \mathrm{~Hz}$

Angular velocity for rotational motion is given by

$$\begin{aligned} & \omega=2 \pi f \\ & \therefore \quad \omega_1=2 \pi t_1=2 \pi \times 10=20 \pi \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \\ & \text { and } \omega_2=2 \pi f_2=2 \pi \times 20=40 \pi \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}$$

According to work-energy theorem,

work done in rotation = change in rotational kinetic energy

$$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad W & =\frac{1}{2} l \omega_2^2-\frac{1}{2} l \omega_1^2 \quad\left[\because K E_{\text {rotational }}=\frac{1}{2} / \omega^2\right] \\ & =\frac{1}{2} l\left(\omega_2^2-\omega_1^2\right)\quad\text{.... (i)} \end{aligned}$$

where, $I=$ moment of inertia of the flywheel.

Substituting given values in Eq. (i), we get

$$\begin{aligned} 12000 & =\frac{1}{2} l\left(1600 \pi^2-400 \pi^2\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad & =\frac{1}{2} l(1200 \times 10) \quad\left[\because \pi^2=10\right] \\ \Rightarrow \quad I & =\frac{12000 \times 2}{12000}=2 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

en.content: The maximum wavelength of radiation emitted by a star is 289.8 nm . Then intensity of radiation for the star is (Given : Stefan's constant $=5.67 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{Wm}^{-2} \mathrm{~K}^{-4}$, Wien's constant, $b=2898 \mu \mathrm{mK}$ )
en.explanation:
$$\begin{aligned} &\text { Given, maximum wavelength, }\\ &\begin{aligned} \lambda_m & =289.8 \mathrm{~nm}=289.8 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m} \\ & =2898 \times 10^{-10} \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$$

Stefan's constant, $\sigma=5.67 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{Wm}^{-2} \mathrm{~K}^{-4}$

Wien's constant, $b=2898 \mu \mathrm{mK}=2898 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{mK}$

According to Wien's displacement law, the maximum wavelength is given by

$$\lambda_m=\frac{b}{T} \Rightarrow T=\frac{b}{\lambda_m}\quad\text{.... (i)}$$

Substituting given values in Eq. (i), we get

$$T=\frac{2898 \times 10^{-6}}{2898 \times 10^{-10}}=10^4 \mathrm{~K}\quad\text{.... (ii)}$$

According to Stefan's law, the energy radiated from a source is given by

$$E=\sigma A e T^4\quad\text{.... (iii)}$$

where, $A=$ area of source

$e=$ emissivity (value between 0 to 1)

The intensity of radiations emitted is equal to energy radiated from a given surface area, i.e.,

$$I=\frac{E}{A}=\sigma e T^4 \quad\text{[from Eq. (iii)]}$$

As e is very small, so

$$I=\sigma T^4\quad\text{.... (iv)}$$

Substituting the value of $T$ from Eq. (ii) in Eq. (iv), we get

$$\begin{aligned} I= & \sigma\left(10^4\right)^4=5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 10^{16} \\ & {\left[\because \sigma=5.67 \times 10^{-8} \text { (given) }\right] } \\ & =5.67 \times 10^8 \mathrm{Wm}^{-2} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A lift is tied with thick iron ropes having mass ' $M$ '. The maximum acceleration of the lift is ' $a$ ' $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ and maximum safe stress is ' S ' $\mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^2$. The minimum diameter of the rope is
en.explanation:
The maximum stress produced in a rope is given by

$$\sigma_{\max }=\frac{\text { Force }}{\text { Area }}=\frac{M g}{\pi r^2}$$

As the lift is accelerating with acceleration a, then

$$\begin{aligned} &\begin{aligned} & \sigma_{\max }=\frac{M(g \pm a)}{\pi r^2} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad r^2=\frac{M(g \pm a)}{\pi S} \quad\text { [Given, } \sigma_{\max }=S \text { ] } \\ & \frac{d^2}{4}=\frac{M(g \pm a)}{\pi S} \quad {\left[\because r=\frac{d}{2}\right]} \\ & \Rightarrow d=\sqrt{\frac{4 M(g \pm a)}{\pi S}} \end{aligned}\\ &\text { As acceleration is maximum i.e., } g^{\prime}=g+a \text {, so }\\ &d=\sqrt{\frac{4 M(g+a)}{\pi S}} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: In Balmer series, wavelength of first line is ' $\lambda_1$ ' and in Brackett series wavelength of first line is ' $\lambda_2$ ' then $\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}$ is
en.explanation:
The wavelength of a line in Balmer series is given by

$$\frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{2^2}-\frac{1}{n^2}\right)\quad [\text{for } n=3,4,5, \ldots]$$

where, $R=$ Rydberg constant.

For first line, $n=3$

$$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{\lambda_1}=R\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9}\right) \Rightarrow \lambda_1=\frac{36}{5 R}\quad\text{.... (i)}$$

The wavelength of a line in Brackett series is given by

$$\frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{4^2}-\frac{1}{n^2}\right)\quad \text{for } n=5,6,7 \ldots$$

For first line, $n=5$

$$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{\lambda_2}=R\left(\frac{1}{16}-\frac{1}{25}\right) \Rightarrow \lambda_2=\frac{400}{9 R}\quad\text{.... (ii)}$$

Dividing Eq. (i) by Eq. (ii), we get

$$\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}=\frac{36}{5 R} \times \frac{9 R}{400}=\frac{81}{500}=0.162$$

en.content: An alternating voltage is given by $E=100 \sin \left(\omega+\frac{\pi}{6}\right) \mathrm{V}$. The voltage will be maximum for the first time when is [ $T=$ periodic time)
en.explanation:
Given, alternating voltage is

$$E=100 \sin \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{6}\right) V$$

The voltage will be maximum, when

$$\begin{aligned} & \sin \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=1 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \sin \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\sin \frac{\pi}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow \omega t+\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\pi}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \omega t=\frac{\pi}{3} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad t=\frac{\pi}{3 \omega}=\frac{\pi \times T}{3 \times 2 \pi} \quad\left[\because \omega=\frac{2 \pi}{T}\right] \\ & =\frac{T}{6} \end{aligned}$$

Thus, the voltage will be maximum for the first time when $t=\frac{T}{6}$.
